full_judgment:
3. The pivotal question which arises for consideration in these matters is whether the Administrator of Waqfs can accord sanction for transferring any part of the Waqf property by way of lease exceeding 5(five) years in exercise of its power under section 56 of the Waqfs Ordinance, 1962 or in the alternative, a mutawalli of a waqf estate can transfer by lease in perpetuity any part of the waqf property with prior approval of the Administrator. An opinion on the point requires consideration of the facts which are succinctly narrated below: 

 Appellant is a mutawalli of a Waqf Estate who instituted Title Suit No. 26 of 1992 (the plaintiff) against the respondent Nos.1-3 seeking nullity of lease deed dated 18th May, 1965 executed by his father Ahidulla as mutawalli of the waqf eatate in favour of respondent Nos. 1 (the defendant) on the ground that his father though executed the lease deed in respect of the suit land measuring an area of 0.92 acre, he did not pay the salami and rent and also did not take over possession of the suit land and thus, the defendant violated the terms of the lease deed, and that the lease was not acted upon. Defendant also instituted Title Suit No. 38 of 1992 seeking declaration of title in respect of 1st schedule land and for recovery of khas possession in respect of 2nd schedule land measuring an area of 0.04 (0.03) acre. His case is that the plaintiff's father Ashidulla, the mutawalli, with prior sanction of the Administrator of Waqfs leased out 0.92 acre of land of plot No.932 at a premium of Taka 300 and handed over possession on the same day. He developed the land and constructed houses in a portion of the land. He also purchased 0.04 acre of land of plot No. 933 situated contiguous to the suit plot for path way and mutated his name, paid rent and taxes to the authorities and thereafter, he was dispossessed from the 2nd schedule of land taking advantage of his temporary absence from the suit land. Appellant's defence case in the latter suit is similar to that of his plaint case and vice versa. 

 6. It was urged on behalf of the appellant that the High Court Division misconstrued section 56 of the Waqfs Ordinance, 1962 and illegally held that a mutawalli of a waqf estate can transfer a portion of the waqf property by lease exceeding five years in failing to notice that such lease tantamount to absolute transfer which is not intended by the legislature. It was further urged that the Administrator has power to accord sanction of grant of lease for a limited period, inasmuch as, the use of coma (,) after the word 'exchange' in sub-section (1) of section 56, and the use of words 'or by way of lease for a term exceeding 5 years' thereafter manifestly suggest that a mutawalli has no power even, with prior sanction of the Administrator to grant lease of any part of the waqf property in perpetuity. 

 9. What's more, I find no inconsistency between the two provisions. Section 33 deals with the power of the Administrator to transfer waqf property when he is in charge of such property in the absence of the mutawalli. This section is found in chapter III, whereas, section 56 is found in Chapter VI under the heading 'Transfer of Waqfs Property.' These two chapters provide for two distinct purposes. It is established principle that the duty of the Court is to effectuate the purpose of an enactment and not to defeat it. In Bates, (1965)1 WLR 1133 (1147), Lord Denning, MR stated the object is to ascertain the intention of the legislature. This intention must be discovered, of course, from the words which they have used but the words must be sensibly interpreted. We are not here to make nonsense of them. If we look at the history, the practice of grouping sections of an Act under different headings was first introduced in UK in 1845 in the Clauses Consolidation Acts (Thring, Practical legislation, Ed.1902). According to Maxwell on the Interpretation of Statutes, 12th Edn. page 11, the headings pre-fixed to sections or sets of sections in some modern statutes are regarded as preambles of those sections. They cannot control the plain words of the statute but they may explain ambiguous words'. Head notes may, in some cases, be looked upon in the light of preambles if there is any ambiguity in the meaning of the sections on which they throw light. The arrangement of sections into parts and their headings are substantive parts of the Act and as is pointed out by Craies on Statute Law, 5th Edn, page 165, 'they are gradually winning recognition as a kind of preamble to the enactments which they precede limiting or explaining their operations'. The above views make no hesitation in arriving at the conclusion that sections 33 and 56 deal with different subjects showing operation in separate fields and are not intended to overlap so as to restrict each other. 

 10. We have the privilege of hearing Mr Mahmudul Islam as amicus curiae. Learned amicus curiae argued that sections 33 and 56 do not conflict with each other for, the sections are found in two chapters for different objects. Section 56 does not restrict permanent lease by a mutawalli provided that the mutawalli has obtained previous sanction of the Administrator. In this connection he has referred to the proviso to sub-section (1) of section 56 which, according to him, manifests that the bar is qualified by the words in contravention of any other law. Mr Islam contended that if such transfer by way of sale, gift, mortgage, exchange or lease for a period exceeding 5 years is barred by any existing law in force then notwithstanding the previous sanction of the Administrator, the transfer would be invalid. He has referred the cases of State of Rajasthan vs Sripal Jain, AIR 1963 SC 1323 and Rohit Pulp and Paper Mills Ltd. vs Collector of Central Excise, Baroda, (1990) 3 SCC 447 in support of his contention. According to Mr Islam, the words used in both sections are clear enough to come to the conclusion that there is no scope to give any statutory interpretation by restricting the power of the Waqfs Administrator. Mr Islam finally contended that the generic words used in section 33 should receive a limited interpretation by reason of its context by legitimately drawing upon the noscitur a sociis principle. In the other words, it is submitted that the restricted words used in the section should be interpreted by applying the principle of 'noscitur a sociis' or on the analogy of the 'ejusdem generis' principle 

 13. In State of Bombay vs Hospital Mazdoor  Savha, AIR 1960 SC 610, the question involved was that two employees of a chain of hospitals were removed and in their place two state servants were appointed. The retrenched employees filed a writ of mandamus directing to rein-statement in their posts on the ground that the retrenchment was void as it did not comply the provisions of sections 25F and 25H of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947. The petition was resisted on the ground that the writ petition was not maintainable, inasmuch as, the hospitals did not constitute an 'industry' and so, the relevant provisions of law were not applicable. The question involved in the appeal for consideration is whether group of hospitals constitutes an 'industry'. The writ petition was ultimately allowed on the reasoning that the orders had not complied the mandatory provisions of law. On appeal from the said judgment it was raised that the definition of 'industry' defined in section 2(j) of the said Act is so wide denotation, 'hospitals' can be excluded from the definition. It was urged that in construing the definition, the Court must adopt the rule of construction 'noscuntur a sociis'. 

 22. On a plain reading of section 56 we find no ambiguity in the language used therein with the language used in section 33 of the Ordinance. There is no doubt on reading section 33 as a whole about the meaning of the words used therein which can be ascertained by reference to the meaning of words associated with it. Therefore, we need not draw upon the noscitur a sociis is or ejusdem generis principles. Section 33 restricts the Administrator in transferring any part of a waqf property while he is in charge of the said property. He can transfer the property for the welfare of the estate with prior permission of the Government. Whereas, the substance of sub-section (1) of section 56 is that a mutawalli can transfer any part of a waqf property in any manner as provided therein but the only restriction is in respect of lease for a period exceeding five years. In such case previous permission of the Waqfs Administrator is necessary. Even if any transfer by way of lease is made for a period exceeding five years with-out sanction of the Administrator, such transfer can be declared void by the Civil Court only on the prayer of the Administrator. Sub-section (4) makes the thing more clear, which provides that even if a mutawalli transfers any property in contravention of sub-section (1) and afterwards he becomes the owner of the property, he may re-convey the property on the direction of the Administrator. It is also provided in sub-section (5) that if any transfer is made in contravention of sub-section (1), such transfer shall be deemed to be an act of malfeasance. 

 24. In the proviso to sub-section (1) of section 56, it is stated that even if there is previous sanction such transfer shall not be validated if it is in contravention of any other law, that is, if any other law prohibits such transfer, any lease exceeding five years even with the previous sanction of the Administrator shall be invalid. Now it is to be looked into whether the lease in question has been granted in violation of any existing law, that is, the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act, 1949 (Act, 1949) and the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 (Act, 1950). The answer to this point depends upon the determination of the nature of the land transferred and the application of those laws in the context of the execution of the deed in question. Admittedly, the suit land is situated within Sylhet City Corporation area and the nature of the suit land has been mentioned as (Bangla) (vegetable garden). Thus the suit land is non-agricultural land. 'Non-agricultural land' within section 2(4) of the Act, 1949 means "land which is used for purposes not connected with agriculture or horticulture and includes any land which is held on lease for the purposes not connected with agriculture or horticulture irrespective of whether it is used for any such purpose...... 

 25. A land which was originally leased for agricultural or horticultural purposes but is being used for purposes not connected with agriculture or horticulture without the consent of the landlord and if the period for which the land has been so used is less than twelve years will not be included in the category of 'non-agricultural land' in view of section 2(4)(b). This exception is not applicable to this case in view of the admitted fact that the lease was granted not for a period less than twelve years. So the primary test in determining a particular land is non-agricultural or not, rests firstly as to whether the land is a 'non-agricultural land' as defined in the Act of 1949, and secondly, the purpose for which the tenancy was created. 

 28. The defendant's tenancy was created after the Act of 1949 came into force in 1965, and therefore, he was an under-tenant within the meaning of Act, 1949 during the relevant times. Section 4 provided the purpose for which a non-agricultural tenant may hold non-agricultural land i.e. for (a) homestead or residential purposes; (b) manufacturing or business purposes; or (c) religious or other purposes. The word 'homestead' includes gardens, tanks and land necessary for enjoyment as home-stead. Under section 2(14) of the Act, 1950, the word 'homestead' means a dwelling house with the land under it, together with any court-yard, garden, tank, place of worship and private burial or cremation ground attached and appertaining to such dwelling house, and includes any out-buildings used for the purpose of enjoying the dwelling house or for purposes connected with agricultural or horticulture and such lands within well-defined limits, whether vacant or not, as are treated to be appertaining thereto. 

 31. Since there is no allegation of violation of section 6 no discussion on this provision is called for. Section 7 provides the rights and liabilities of the tenants in respect of a tenancy created before or after the commencement of the Transfer of Property Act, and in case of a lease created in writing for a period not less than twelve years, and if the landlord has allowed the tenant to raise constructions or structures before the expiry period of lease, then the ten-ant holding the non-agricultural land shall not be ejected by the landlord on any grounds other than for the purposes specified in the section. In case of death of the tenant his heirs shall inherit the tenanted property. These protections provided to an under-tenant in Chapter IV would be applicable to the defendant if section 26A had not been inserted in the Act of 1949 in 1967 but the scenario has totally been changed after the amendment. 

 32. Section 23 of the Act provides the manner of transfer of non-agricultural land. It is provided that every transfer of the non-agricultural land by a non-agricultural tenant shall be made by registered instrument. The lease in question was executed by a registered instrument and thus, the lease satisfied the requirements of section 23. There is another aspect which is very much important for resolving the dispute in controversy. After the acquisition of rent receiving interest, there was restriction for sub-letting of any land by section 75A of the Act, 1950 which was inserted by Act XII of 1954. Under this provision the creation of a subordinate tenancy was prohibited and/or invalidated. Under the amendment the rent-receivers were themselves to retain certain classes of retainable khas land as tenant directly under the Government. They were restricted to create further sub-tenancies under them. The creation of sub-tenancy was validated which were effected before the publication of the Notification under sections 17(3) or 31(1) of the said Act. Similar prohibition for sub-letting has been provided in section 26A (1) of Act, 1949 by the East Pakistan Ordinance No. IX of 1967, which provides, Notwithstanding anything contained in this Act or in any other law for the time being in force or in any contract, no non-agricultural tenant shall sub-let the whole or any part of his tenancy on any terms or conditions whatsoever. 

 34. A rent receiver within the meaning of section 2(23) of Act, 1950 includes a proprietor or a tenure-holder and a raiyat, underraiyat or a non-agricultural tenant whose land has been let out and also the immediate landlord of a person who holds any land free of rent in consideration of some service to be rendered. Therefore, we find that a non-aquiculture ten-ant has been included in the category of a rent-receiver in the said Act. In the Act, 1949, the expression 'raiyat' or 'rent-receiver' has not been used or defined and in its place, the term a 'tenant' or an 'under-tenant' has been used. On a combined reading of these provisions, we find that the expressions of "raiyat" or a "tenant" are genus and an under-raiyat' or a 'sub-tenant' or an 'under-tenant' are species. The rent receiving interest of a raiyat passes to the Government after the acquisition of receiving interest and the rent-receiver accrued the right to receive compensation. Similarly a tenant under the Act of 1949 becomes a rent-receiver when his land has been let out to another per-son who holds it on a contract to pay rent after section 26A comes into effect. 

 35. Next the question to be considered is whether in view of section 70 of Act, 1949, the defendant can be evicted by the plaintiff in execution of a decree of civil Court. Section 70 pro-vides non-agricultural tenant shall be ejected from the tenancy or from any non-agricultural land which he holds except in execution of a decree of a competent civil Court". This provision clearly suggests that a non-agricultural tenant can be evicted by the landlord through a decree of a civil Court. This section is in part materia with section 89 of Bengal Tenancy Act. The effect of this section is to limit the landlord the right of ejectment under the Act. This section was in existence in the original Act of 1949 with a view to protect the tenants from being evicted by the landlords from non-agricultural land other than by due process of law. This section becomes obsolete after section 26A has come into force. 

 36. Section 83 of Act, 1950 provides that a raiyat shall have the right to occupy and use the land comprised in his holding in any manner he likes. With the acquisition of lands of different classes of rent receivers, rent receiving interest extends up to the end of Part IV. The second division starts with Part V and extends upto the end of Act, 1950. Different provisions of Part V became operative in different areas or districts from the date of publication of notifications and thereupon Bengal Tenancy Act stood repealed on those areas or districts. All holders of land within the areas in respect of which compensation assessment-roll has been published, became tenants under the Government. Section 81A of Act, 1950 provides rights and liabilities of non-agricultural tenants. It says; 

 "(1) Except as otherwise provided in this Part, the rights and liabilities a holder of non-agricultural land, who has become a tenant under the Government in respect of such land by virtue of the acquisition of the superior right in such-land under the pro-visions of this Act, shall, where the provisions of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act, 1949, applied to such land, at the time of such acquisition, be regulated by provisions of that Act. 

 39. If a non-agricultural tenant sub-lets his tenancy or a part thereof in contravention of subsection (1), the tenancy shall be extinguished and shall vest in the Government as per sub-section (2) of section 26A. When the lease under consideration was created this pro-vision was nonexistent. As observed above, the defendant was an under-tenant when the tenancy was created. Now the question for consideration is to determine the status of the defendant after insertion of section 26A. On a combined reading of sections 81 and 82(8), there is no gainsaying that a sub-tenant or under-tenant created by a tenant has matured his status as a tenant/malik under the Act of 1949 on and from the date of section 26A coming into force. 40. In Province of East Pakistan vs Muhammad Hossain, 16 DLR (SC) 667, the question arose for consideration was whether after the acquisition of rent receiving interest, a tenancy created by a rent-receiver in respect Of non-agricultural land is hit by section 75A or in the alternative there is conflict between section 9 and 75A of the Act. It was observed by H. Rahman, J. 'Section 75A, though it came into force on the 30th August 1954, was made operative only from the date or notification under section 11 (3) or section 31 (1) and, as such, it had no retrospective operation and did not invalidate leases created before such date." Similar principle will be applicable to the case of defendant whose lease was created prior to the insertion of section 26A. 

 42. The purpose of omitting the word 'sub-lease' by Ordinance IX of 1967 as evident is only for the purpose of avoiding preemption under section 24 of the Act. In the said Act the word 'sub-let' has not been defined. Only the word 'under-tenant' has been defined in section 3(3). The use of the expression 'sublet' in my view is misnomer, inasmuch as, if we read this provision along with sections 3, 21 and 22, the intention of the Legislature will be discernible. The expression 'sub-lease' or 'sublet' have been used in the same context of the term 'under-tenant' and they are used in cognate sense. A sub-ordinate tenancy under which an under-tenant would be liable to pay for that land to a person other than the Government is liable pay to the Government after section 26A came into force and his status has been upgraded to a tenant/malik. In other words, after insertion of section 26A by Ordinance No.IX of 1967, there is one category of non-agricultural tenant on and from 22nd December, 1967 and the defendant is a tenant/malik under the Government and whatever right the plaintiff had in respect of the suit land extinguished from that date. Thus, there is no violation of section 26A or any other provisions of the Act, 1949 or Act, 1950. Now the rights which have been given to a raiyat under section 83 of the Act, 1950 can also be exercised by a under-tenant created before 1967, such as, to occupy and use the non-agricultural land in any manner he likes. 

 44. Mr Bhuiyan contended that even if it is assumed that the Administrator accorded sanction, such sanction was obtained mechanically without holding any inquiry and giving notice to the persons affected by the transfer and also without hearing the parties and as such, the sanction is not a sanction in the eye of law. Therefore, the lease, according to him, is violative to section 57 of the Waqfs Ordinance. This point is devoid of substance, inasmuch as, neither in the plaint nor at any stage of the proceeding the plaintiff has raised this point. The learned counsel has raised this point for the first time before this Division. If such point had been raised at the initial stage of the proceedings, the defendant would have been able to prove that the lease was granted following the procedures by calling the record from the office of the Waqfs Administrator. Moreso, in the recital of the deed there are averments that as the residential houses of the Waqf Estate were in a dilapidated condition and could not be repaired due to shortage of fund, the land was leased out for the welfare of the Waqf Estate with prior sanction the Waqfs Administrator. Therefore, the lease was granted for the benefit and welfare of the Waqf Estate and also for the purpose of fulfilling the objects for which the waqf was created. 

 45. An Administrator is appointed by the Government in exercise of powers conferred under section 7 of the Waqfs Ordinance. Section 10 of the Ordinance states that the Administrator shall be deemed to be a public officer with-in the meaning of the Code of Civil Procedure. Naturally he is a public servant and he has accorded the sanction while discharging public duties as a public servant. There is presumption of regularity of the official acts by a person in discharge of his official duty until the contrary is proved. The court, in the absence of anything to the contrary, may presume that such permission was accorded after holding a proper inquiry in accordance with law. Over and above, since the plaintiff has no right or interest in the suit land, he has no locus standi to raise question about the legality of the lease. 

 49. The Court of Appeal below committed another fundamental error in assuming that no lease of immovable property could be granted other than a lease for occupation of the land for a limited period. Further, the Court of Appeal below compared creation of the tenancy with the settlement of land made by ex-landlords under the Bengal Tenancy Act, 1985 on a misconception of law. The Court of Appeal below ought to have ascertained the nature of the land, the laws applicable to such lease and the construction of the deed before deciding the question on whether the mutawalli of a waqf estate has power, to transfer a portion of the waqf property by way of lease for a period exceeding 5 years. As observed above, the lease was created in respect of non-agricultural land. A tenant holding non-agricultural land under a lease in writing for a period exceeding twelve years shall not be ejected by the landlord on any grounds other than the grounds specified in section 4 of Act 1949 and his interest shall, in case of death, be devolved upon his heirs in view of clauses (i) and (ii) respectively of sub-section (3) of section 7. Similarly in case of a tenancy created to an 'under-tenant' corresponding rights of protection have been given be sections 20, 21 and 22 of the Act, 1949. 

 51. In the case of leases for agricultural or manufacturing purposes, the presumption will be that they are from year to year and in the case of other leases the tenancy is deemed to be from month to month. In the former case a six month's notice is necessary for terminating lease and in the latter case fifteen days notice is necessary. These provisions are quite distinguishable and not applicable to the case of the defendant in view of the discussions made above. The Court of Appeal below approached the matter on wrong premise in considering the lease in question and such wrong approach had reflected in the latter part of the judgment. It has not explained why a lease of non-agricultural land granted with prior sanction of the Administrator in respect of any part of Waqf property by the mutawalli for the welfare of the waqf estate would be illegal. The High Court Division on consideration of section 56 of the Ordinance has rightly approved the views of the trial Court. The High Court Division held that the lease having been created with prior sanction of the Administrator was legal and valid. Accordingly, the High Court Division has rightly found that the plaintiff's suit is not maintainable and is liable to be dismissed. 

 55. The case of the plaintiff as made out in the plaint, in short, was that after the death of his father, Asidullah, he became the Mutawalli of Reazullah Waqf Estate (EC No.12876) and continued to be in possession of the land of the waqf estate. Reazullah Waqf Estate is the owner of the second schedule 1 and to the plaint along with other lands and the said lands were recorded in the name of the mutawalli of the Waqf Estate, Asidullah, the predecessor mutawalli. For protection of the lands of the waqf estate, a lease deed was executed and registered on May 18, 1965 by Asidullah in favour of defendant No. 1 (hereinafter referred to as the defendant) in respect of the second schedule land at a Nazrana of Taka 300 and at the yearly rent of taka 40-00. But the defendant during the life time of the predecessor-mutawalli, Asidullah and after his death did not pay the Nazrana and the yearly rent and thus did not fulfill the terms of the lease. Since the death of Asidullah, the plaintiff is in possession of the land described in the second schedule to the plaint. The defendant did not get possession of the land leased out to him and thus the lease deed was not acted upon and that the Lease of the land described in the second schedule to the plaint was a mere paper transaction. The defendant taking the advantage of the non-effective lease deed got his name mutated in the revenue records in collusion with defendant 

 57. In the plaint, it was averred that along with the other lands, the first schedule land belonged to Riaz Ullah Waqf Estate, enrolled as E.G. No. 12876 and the same was recorded in the name of the late , Asidullah, the then Mutwalli, father of the present Mutawalli Md. Kalimullah. Defendant No.1 as plaintiff earlier filed Title Suit No.26 of 1992 in the same Court. Former Mutwalli,  Asidullah by taking prior sanction from the Administrator of Waqfs, vide his Memo No. 2270 dated 15-5-1965 granted lease of 92 decimals of land out of dag No.932 and 08 decimals of land out of dag No. 923 at a Nazrana of Taka 300. The lessee paid the Nazrana to the mutawalli-Asidullah on 18-5-1965, on which date lease deed was executed and registered in between the parties and possession of the lease hold land was handed over to the lessee, who continued to be in peaceful possession thereof in his own right. The plaintiff purchased 4 decimals of land from the adjacent dag No.933 from its owner Amzadullah by registered deed dated 21-12-1965 and opened a pathway over there for peaceful enjoyment of his leasehold land and then he brought Mutation Case No.5/1973-74 and DP Khatian No.1/234 was opened in his name. Later the plaintiff by filing Miscellaneous Case No.2/ 1987-88 prayed for inclusion of his name in the printed khatian where the present Mutawalli filed objection and the matter being heard in presence of both sides, the name of the plaintiff was entered in Chhapa khatian No.230 and he continued to possess by paying rents to the Government and re-claimed some portions thereof, planted fruit bearing trees and vegetables and also dug a well for water and has been in possession thereof for over more than the period of limitation. The 'plaintiff also sold a part of the land in 1978 to one Moulana Solaiman, one of the defendants who being in possession engaged a caretaker, namely: Mukibur Rahman who started residing there with his brother, Maznur Rahman and they in collusion with the son of the former Mutawalli denied the title of Moulana Solaiman, who then brought Title Suit No.26 of 1990 in the Court of Assistant Judge for eviction of the aforesaid two brothers from his land. After the death of former mutawalli-Asidullah in 1979, his son Kalimullah, defendant No.1 (plaintiff of Title Suit No.26 of 1992) became the Mutawalli of the waqf estate and he in collusion with the owner of the adjacent dag Nos.922 and 929 tried to cut away earth forcibly by entering into dag No. 932, the plaintiff brought Title Suit No.38 of 1988 in the Court of Assistant Judge against defendant No.1 and others for permanent injunction and got an order of ad-interim injunction against them. But defendant No. 1 in collusion with defendant Nos.7-12 in order to grab the suit property and taking the advantage of the absence of the plaintiff dispossessed him from 3(three) decimals of land as described in the second schedule to the plaint and hurriedly erected 4(four) ekchala chhapra; hence the plaintiff was compelled to file the suit for the aforementioned reliefs. 

 59. The plaintiff of Title Suit No.26 of 1992 who was defendant No.1 in Title Suit No.38 of 1992 contested the same by filing a written statement denying the material allegations of the plaint and contending, inter alia, the facts as were stated in the plaint of Title suit No.26 of 1992. The plaintiff of Title suit No. 38 of 1992 as defendant also contested Title Suit No.26 of 1992 by filing written statement denying the material allegations inter alia, the facts as stated in the plaint of Title Suit No.38 of 1992 

 "The learned Counsel for the petitioner submits that the learned Judge of the High Court Division failed to correctly interpret the provisions of section 56 of the Ordinance relating to power of the Administrator of Waqf (sic) to accord sanction to transfer immovable property of Waqf Estate by way of lease for a term exceeding 5 years in that section 56 of the Waqf Ordinance having barred transfer of such property by way of sale, gift, mortgage or exchange cannot be interpreted to have conferred power on the Administrator to sanction perpetual lease of the Waqf property which amounts to absolute transfer not intended by the legislature and therefore, the Administrator can be said to have power to accord sanction to grant lease beyond 5 years but for a limited period and not a lease in perpetuity and therefore, the judgment of the High Court Division is not sustainable in law." 

 64. Mr Abdul Wadud Bhuiyan, learned Counsel, appearing for the appellant, has submitted that the learned Judge of the Single Bench of the High Court Division erroneously interpreted the provisions of section 56 of the Waqf Ordinance, shortly, the Ordinance as to the power of the Administrator of Waqfs to accord sanction to transfer immovable property of the Waqf Estate by way of lease for a term exceeding 5(five) years. He has further submitted that section 56 of the Ordinance having barred transfer of waqf property by way of lease by the mutawalli for more than 5 (five) years without the sanction of the Administrator of Waqfs cannot be interpreted to have conferred power on the Administrator of Waqfs to give sanction for perpetual lease of any property of the waqf, because such sanction would amount to absolute transfer which was not intended by the legislature and hence, the permanent lease given by the mutawalli Asidullah vide lease deed No.5679 dated 18-5-1965 in favour of defendant No.1 was void and by such lease he did not acquire any right and title therein. Mr. Bhuiyan, by referring to section 57 of the Ordinance, has further submitted that the Administrator of Waqfs acted illegally in giving sanction to the mutawalli to lease out the suit property inasmuch as before such sanction no inquiry as required by the said section was held. He has lastly submitted that the Appellate  Court being the last Court of fact, on consideration of the evidence, came to the clear finding that the lease deed No.5679 executed on 18-5-1965 did not take legal effect, the learned Judge of the Single Bench erred in law in setting aside the judgment and decree of the Appellate Court without setting aside the said; hiding of fact arrived at by the said Court and therefore, the impugned judgment and order is liable to be set-aside. 

 65. In support of his contentions Mr Bhuiyan has referred to the cases of AK Gopalan vs State of Madras AIR 1950, SC 27 and Hafizuddin Ahmed vs M Aslam Minh, 55 DLR 95. 

 69. From the judgment of the trial Court, it appears that though both suits were disposed of by a common judgment, it decided the merit of the suit separately and decided the merit of Title Suit No. 26 of 1992 first. The trial Court dismissed Title Suit No.26 of 1992 on the finding, inter alia, that (i) defendant No.1 (plaintiff of Title Suit No.38 of 1992) got possession of the lease hold land from the lessor pursuant to the lease deed dated 18-5-1965. In coming to the said finding the trial Court considered the kabala dated 21-12-1965 being No.5384, exhibit-K(1) by which defendant No.1 purchased 4 (four) decimals of land from the adjacent plot being plot number 933, rent receipts: exhibits-'Kha and Kha(1)' by which he paid rents in respect of the land in question upto 1379-1382 and exhibit- 'Ga' the certified copies of the order sheets of the mutation proceedings, (ii) the lease deed of defendant No.1 dated 18-5-1965 is valid and is in existence and he produced sufficient documentary evidence in sup-port of his claim of acquisition of title in the leasehold land, (iii) The plaintiff failed to prove his title and possession in the second schedule land, (iv) the defendant acquired his valid title in the second schedule land by virtue of the lease deed dated 18-5-1965 and he is in possession thereof, but not in its entire area and he also failed to prove his possession in any particular direction (in Bangla it has been stat এবং তাহার দখল কোন দিকে আছে তাহা সুনির্দিষ্ট ভাবে প্রমানিত হয় নাই।) (v) The plaintiff failed to prove his possession in the second schedule land, so he was not entitled to get the decree as prayed for and (vi) the suit was barred by limitation and was also not maintainable in its present form. 

 71. From the judgment of the Appellate Court, it appears that it allowed Title Appeal No.57 of 1995 (this appeal was filed against the judgment and decreed passed in Title Suit No.26 of 1992) on the view that section 56 of the Ordinance did not authorise the mutawalli of a waqf estate to lease out its immovable property permanently. The Appellate Court further held that though exhibit-'Kha' showed that the Administrator of Waqfs gave sanction to the then mutawalli-Asidullah, the father of the plaintiff to lease out the land in question of the waqf permanently, the Administrator of Waqf had no power to give such sanction under section 56 of the Ordinance. The Appellate Court further held that the defendant failed to file any receipt showing payment of rent to the waqf estate and by mutating his name as apparent from exhibit-'Kha', he did not acquire any title to the lease hold land and the evidence adduced by the defendant as to his possession in the said land and then dispossession from the second schedule land did not prove his exclusive possession therein. 

 72. As stated earlier, the High Court Division sent Title Suit No.38 of 1992 back on remand to the trial Court for writing out a fresh judgment on the question of possession and dispossession only as made out by the plaintiff in the plaint in the light of the observations made in the judgment. From the impugned judgment and order, it appears that about the finding of possession of the trial Court as well as the Appellate Court, the High Court Division observed as follows: "with regard to possession, the trial Court appears to have considered the oral evidence and came to a finding that 'opposite party No.1 failed to prove his possession and that the petitioner was in possession in one part of his judgment but at the conclusion it held the possession of the petitioner was not definitely and clearly proved. Upon such view, the trial Court dismissed the suit of the petitioner. Appellate Court appears to have considered no oral evidence at all. The conclusion of the appellate court on possession is influenced by its wrong decision on the deed of lease. Such finding on possession based on total 'non-reading of the evidence oral and documentary on record cannot also be sustained in law." 

 "That the appeal be partly allowed on contest against the defendant-respondent No.1 and ex-parte against the rest without costs. The impugned judgment and decree passed by the learned Court below are hereby set aside. The plaintiff-appellants' title over the suit land is hereby declared. The appellants' prayer for recovery of khas possession against the defendant-respondents in respect of 0.03 decimals of land is also allowed. The defendant-respondents are hereby directed to vacate the said land and deliver the possession of the same to the plaintiff appellants by peaceful means as stated in the 2nd schedule of the plaint within 90(Ninety) days from the date of this orders, violation of which shall be seriously dealt with in accordance with law. At the same time, the plaintiff appellants after the expiry of those days, could recover the khas possession of the same by the aid and assistance of the lawful means through the court concerned. 

 74. Defendant of Title Suit No. 38 of 1992 (plaintiff of Title Suit No. 26 of 1992), that is, the present appellant filed Civil Revision No.170 of 2004 before the High Court Division against the judgment and decree passed by the Appellate Court in Title Appeal No.197 of 2002 and the Rule in the civil revision was discharged on the 25th of February, 2007 leading to the filing of the leave, petition (CP No.1568 of 2007). So with the disposal of Title Appeal No.197 of 2002 as affirmed in Civil Revision No.170 of, 2004, by the High Court Division, findings of possession and dispossession given earlier by the Courts below in Title Suit Nos.26 and 38 of 1992 and Title Appeal Nos.57 of 1995 and 182 of 1974 lost all its legal force. In this regard, it is very pertinent to state that the appellant did not file any leave petition against the judgment and order passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision No.2572 of 1998 sending Title Suit No. 38 of 1992 back on remand to the trial Court and thus he allowed Title Suit No.38 of 1992 to be heard and disposed of afresh. And in the instant case, leave has been granted only to decide the point as to whether the learned Judge of the Single Bench correctly interpreted section 56 of the Ordinance as to the power of the Administrator of Waqfs to accord sanction to the mutawalli of the waqf estate to give permanent lease of its immovable property. So, we see no scope of deciding the other points as argued by Mr Abdul Wadud Bhuiyan, namely: that before according sanction to the mutawalli to lease out 92 decimals of land of the waqf estate, no enquiry under section 57 of the Ordinance was held and that defendant No. 1 (Moulana Fariduddin Ahmed) failed to prove that he paid the Nazrana and the yearly rent as per terms of the lease deed as well as question of possession and dispossession as alleged by the deceased defendant (predecessor-in-interest of respondent Nos. l(a) and 1(b). In the context, Mr. Mahbubey Alam rightly pointed out that no issue as to the non holding of enquiry by the Administrator of Waqfs under section 57 of the Ordinance was raised in the Courts below and even before the High Court Division. And such a question being fundamentally a question of fact cannot be decided by this Court as a Court of first instance. 

 76. For our purpose sub-sections (2), (3), (4) and of the section are not relevant as admittedly sanction was accorded to the mutawalli by the Administrator of Waqfs to give permanent lease of 92 decimals of land of plot No.932 of the waqf estate. 

 82. From a mere reading of other words used in sub-section (1) of section 56 of the Ordinance, it is clear that the legislature has created no bar in according sanction by the Administrator of Waqfs to the mutawalli of a waqf estate to transfer its immovable property by way of sale, gift, mortgage or exchange. Transfers by sale, gift, or ex chancre is definitely permanent in nature though as per section 58 of the Transfer of Property Act mortgage is the transfer of an interest in specific "immovable property" for the purpose of securing the payment of money advanced or to be advanced by way of loan, an existing or future debt, or the performance of an engagement which may give rise to a pecuniary liability. So, when in the same section, the Administrator of Waqfs has been given the power to accord sanction to the mutawalli of a waqf to transfer any of its immovable property by way of sale, gift, or exchange then it will be a too narrow interpretation to say that the legislature did not mean to empower the Administrator of Waqfs to accord sanction to a mutawalli to lease out any immovable property of waqf permanently but only of temporary in nature, that is, periodic lease. 

 83. In the context, we may also refer to section 33 of the Ordinance. This section has provided that notwithstanding anything contained elsewhere in the Ordinance or any other law for the time being in force or in any waqf deed or in any contract, the Administrator may, with the previous sanction of the Government, transfer any part of waqf property for the improvement and benefit of the waqf  (emphasis supplied). So, the legislature has not created any absolute bar from transferring any part of the waqf property, but such transfer must be necessary for the improvement and benefit of the waqf. However, we make it very clear that the power conferred upon the Administrator of Waqfs to accord sanction to a mutawalli of a waqf to transfer any immovable property of a waqf by way of sale, gift, mortgage or exchange or by way of lease for a term exceeding five years or permanent (as in the instant case) by section 56(1) of the Ordinance must be subject to fulfillment of the requirement of section 57 thereof. The section has stipulated 3 (three) obligations to be discharged by the Administrator of Waqfs before according sanction to transfer any immovable property of waqf, these are: (a) to make enquiry by himself for the transfer prayed for (b) to give notice to such persons in such manner as the Administrator thinks fit and (c) hearing them (that is the persons so notified), if they desire to be heard. To us, it appears that the enquiry so made must be in the true sense, that is, it must not be mechanical but transparent as to the necessity for transferring any immovable property of the waqf and the notice must be given to all concerned persons of the waqf particularly, the beneficiaries of the waqf and giving fair chance of hearing to the parties involved in the matter. We do not also see any reason for not reading the conditions or limitations as provided in section 33 of the Ordinance in section 56(1) thereof that before granting sanction the Administrator must be satisfied that such transfer is necessary for the improvement and benefit of the waqf and not to cause any injury, waste or loss of the waqf. In the context, we may recall the pleading of the plaintiff that the lease was granted for the protection of the land of the waqf estate. In the facts and circumstances of the instant case as discussed hereinbefore the principle of law enunciated in the cited cases referred by Mr Abdul Wadud Bhuiyan does not help him. Therefore, we find no substance in the submission of Mr Bhuiyan that since the Administrator of Waqfs has not been vested with the power to accord sanction to the mutawalli of a waqf estate to give permanent lease of any immoveable property of the waqf, the lease deed dated 18-5-1965 executed and registered by the deceased mutawalli on the basis of sanction given by the Administrator of Waqfs was void and by such deed defendant No. 1 acquired no right, title and interest in the lease hold land, that is, the suit land.
